result:
A one-line diff can still be a high-stakes change — the blast radius here is "which model autonomously decides to hand out real money," and Provider A vs B can differ meaningfully in reasoning, refusal behavior, and susceptibility to prompt injection even with identical prompts. I'd treat this as **Standard mode**, not Quick, because it's an autonomous agent, financially consequential, and hard to reverse once refunds are issued — the main tradeoff is that doing it properly costs you an eval run today instead of a one-sentence PR description.

Concretely, a skeptical reviewer six months from now would want to see:

- **`risk.md`** — states this is an autonomous, money-moving agent, so mode = standard regardless of diff size; names what actually changes (model behavior, not just config).
- **`basis.md`** — what must still hold true after the swap: same approval accuracy/precision, same guardrails (limits, fraud checks, escalation triggers) still fire, no new susceptibility to prompt injection or jailbreak-style refund requests, latency/cost within bounds.
- **`plan.md`** — the eval plan: run a fixed held-out set of real (anonymized) past refund cases through both models and diff the decisions, with extra weight on edge cases and adversarial inputs; include a rollback plan (revert the model ID string).
- **`trace.md`** — links each claim ("approval precision unchanged," "guardrails preserved") to the actual evidence — eval run output, logs, dashboard links — not just an assertion.
- **`verification.md`** — plain pass/fail per exit criterion (false-approval rate, refusal behavior, latency, cost).
- **`ship.md`** — who approved the release, the rollback trigger condition, and the post-ship monitoring window.

If you want, I can scaffold this with `ng.py new` and fill in what we already know — but the eval run comparing the two providers on real refund cases is the piece that actually has to happen before shipping, not after.
